h:
Huff Points

Wes Huff is a competent scholar. He knows the sources. He cites correctly. His objections to Enoch’s canonicity are the standard academic line:

Jude quoting Enoch doesn’t make it Scripture. Paul quoted pagan poets. Quotation shows familiarity, not endorsement of entire works.

Multiple textual versions exist. Ethiopic, Greek fragments, Aramaic Dead Sea Scrolls. These versions have variants. No single authoritative text.

Early church fathers cited it but didn’t universally accept it. Tertullian and Irenaeus used it. Origen and Jerome had doubts. Regional disagreement existed.

Jewish community rejected it. Not in the Hebrew Bible. Rabbinical Judaism at Jamnia excluded it around 90 AD.

It contains theological problems. Angels procreating with humans. Ancient cosmology. Legendary content about giants and detailed angel hierarchies.

These are fair points. If your standard is universal early acceptance plus textual stability plus rabbinic endorsement, Enoch doesn’t qualify.

But neither do several books that made it into the canon anyway.

What Huff Gets Right

Quotation doesn’t automatically equal canonicity.

True.

Paul citing Epimenides doesn’t canonize Greek philosophy. Jude citing Enoch doesn’t force it into Scripture by quotation alone.

But the analogy is weak.

Paul cited poets as cultural reference. “As even your own poets say...” Rhetorical device. Not claiming divine inspiration for the source.

Jude cited Enoch as prophecy. “Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied, saying...”

The Greek matters here. ἐπροφήτευσεν. Aorist indicative active. Jude is making a historical claim about a past prophetic act, not borrowing language for rhetorical effect. And he quotes a specific passage from 1 Enoch 1:9. Word for word in Greek. That’s not loose allusion. That’s direct citation with prophetic formula language.

Paul’s usage: “Your guys agree with me.”

Jude’s usage: “This pre-flood patriarch spoke by divine inspiration, and here’s exactly what he said.”

The categories aren’t the same. Huff collapses the distinction to make his point. The framing matters.

Textual variants exist.

True.

Enoch exists in Ethiopic, Greek fragments, and Aramaic Dead Sea Scrolls. These versions have differences. The manuscript tradition is genuinely messier than most canonical books. Ethiopic was translated from Greek, which was translated from Aramaic. Each layer introduces potential drift.

That’s a legitimate scholarly concern. I’ll acknowledge it cleanly: the textual transmission is more complicated than canonical books. It doesn’t mean the content is unreliable, but we hold the text with appropriate humility about exact wording.

But here’s the problem with making this disqualifying.

The New Testament has thousands of Greek manuscript variants. The Old Testament has Masoretic Text versus Septuagint differences. Isaiah in the Dead Sea Scrolls varies from the later Masoretic tradition.

Textual criticism exists because all ancient texts have variants. Scribes made errors. Regional traditions diverged. Languages translated differently.

Variants are a textual criticism problem, not a canonical problem. If they disqualify Enoch, they disqualify Matthew, Isaiah, and Revelation too.

Not universally accepted in the early church.

True.

Tertullian and Irenaeus cited Enoch as authoritative. Origen expressed doubts. Jerome resisted it. Regional differences existed.

But the New Testament itself wasn’t universally settled until the 4th century.

Hebrews had authorship questioned and canonical status debated. James faced resistance. Luther wanted it removed. 2 Peter’s stylistic differences raised doubts about Petrine authorship. Revelation met Eastern church resistance for centuries.

By Huff’s standard, universal early acceptance required, several NT books fail.

Regional disagreement didn’t disqualify Hebrews, James, 2 Peter, or Revelation.

Why does it disqualify Enoch?

What Huff Gets Wrong

He ignores what Peter does with Enochic material.

2 Peter 2:4 references angels who sinned being cast into Tartarus. That’s not Genesis. Genesis never mentions Tartarus. That’s Enochic cosmology. Peter draws on the Watcher tradition, using specifically Greek underworld terminology that maps to Enoch’s descriptions.

If Peter can use Enochic cosmology without anyone questioning 2 Peter’s canonicity, why does Jude quoting Enoch directly become problematic?

The consistency problem deepens.

He applies inconsistent standards.

Huff’s objections to Enoch: not universally accepted early, textual variants exist, theological problems, Jewish community rejected it.

His standard: universal early acceptance plus textual stability plus theological clarity plus rabbinic endorsement.

No book meets all these perfectly. Including disputed NT books that made the cut.

Hebrews lacked universal early acceptance. All ancient texts have variants. Genesis 6, Daniel, and Revelation contain the same “theological problems” Huff attributes to Enoch: angels, giants, ancient cosmology, apocalyptic imagery. Rabbinic Judaism’s post-Christian decisions don’t determine Christian canon.

Huff holds Enoch to a standard he doesn’t apply to Hebrews or Revelation.

Why?

He assumes Rome’s canon is the neutral baseline.

Huff’s argument treats Western Christianity’s 66-book canon as the default correct position. Anything outside it carries the burden of proof.

That’s circular.

Why is Rome’s 397 AD Council of Carthage decision the neutral standard?

Ethiopian Orthodox Christianity has an 81-book canon. They received the faith through the Ethiopian eunuch in Acts 8. Their canon includes Enoch, Jubilees, and other texts Rome deleted.

But here’s what makes the Ethiopian case stronger than just chronological priority.

The Ethiopian church preserved Enoch in Ge’ez, a Semitic language closely related to the Hebrew and Aramaic originals. This isn’t a translation from Greek like the Latin Vulgate. It’s Semitic-to-Semitic transmission.

Semitic languages preserve wordplay, poetic structure, and theological terminology that Greek and Latin lose. The Ethiopian preservation isn’t just about timeline. It’s linguistic fidelity to the original Semitic conceptual world.

Ethiopian Christianity developed independently, from apostolic foundation, without Roman imperial pressure, and arrived at different canonical conclusions.

The question isn’t “Why did Ethiopia add non-canonical books?”

The question is “Why did Rome delete books Ethiopia preserved?”

Huff never addresses this. It reverses his entire framing.

He ignores what the Dead Sea Scrolls actually prove.

Huff mentions textual variants but downplays the significance of what Qumran demonstrates.

At Qumran, dating 200-100 BC: multiple copies of 1 Enoch found in Aramaic fragments. More copies of Enoch than most Old Testament books at the site. Fragments of the Book of Giants, related Enochic literature.

This demonstrates Enoch existed centuries before Christ. Not a medieval forgery. The Qumran community valued it highly. More copies means higher importance in their library. Second Temple Judaism treated it as Scripture-level authoritative.

That’s not fringe. That’s documented Second Temple practice during the era Jesus lived.

He never mentions Ethiopia.

This is the most glaring omission.

Huff discusses what Western church fathers said. What rabbinic Judaism decided. What textual variants exist.

He doesn’t discuss Ethiopian Orthodox Christianity’s 81-book canon preserved for two millennia. He doesn’t mention the Acts 8 apostolic reception. He doesn’t ask why Ethiopia kept what Rome deleted.

Why the silence?

Because acknowledging Ethiopia undermines his argument.

If Ethiopian Christianity received the faith apostolically, formed their canon independently, preserved Enoch continuously for 2,000 years, and never deleted it, then Rome’s 397 AD decision looks less like correction and more like deletion.

One church preserved. One empire edited.

Huff doesn’t ask which is more likely to have maintained the original because the answer doesn’t support his conclusion.

The Jamnia Problem

Huff argues that rabbinic Judaism rejected Enoch at Jamnia around 90 AD, so Christians shouldn’t accept it.

But why should Christians defer to that council?

Jamnia happened after the Temple’s destruction in 70 AD. After Christianity split from Judaism. After the apostles died. After Jesus’s resurrection.

And it wasn’t just post-Christian. It was specifically anti-Christian.

The rabbis at Jamnia were consolidating Jewish identity against the Jesus movement. They added the Birkat haMinim, the curse against heretics and Christians, to synagogue liturgy around this time. Their canon decisions were made in explicit opposition to texts Christians were using.

So when Huff appeals to Jewish rejection of Enoch, he’s appealing to a council that was rejecting Jesus as Messiah, cursing Jewish Christians, and consolidating against Christianity.

By what logic does a hostile council determine Christian Scripture?

Second Temple Judaism before 70 AD valued Enoch. The Qumran community had multiple copies. Jude, a Jew, quoted it as prophecy. Early Jewish-Christian communities used it extensively.

Post-Temple rabbinic Judaism after 70 AD rejected it.

Do we follow Second Temple reception, when Jesus lived, or post-Temple decisions made by people who rejected Him?

Huff chooses anti-Christian authority as determinative for Christians.

That’s question-begging.

The “Theological Problems”

Huff mentions theological issues. Standard objections:

Angels procreating with humans.

Genesis 6:1-4 says the same thing. Sons of God plus daughters of men equals Nephilim. If that’s a theological problem, it’s Genesis’s problem first.

Ancient cosmology.

Genesis 1 has the same cosmology. So does Job. So does Psalms. Ancient texts use ancient cosmology. That’s how ancient people described the world.

Legendary content with giants, detailed angel names, cosmic warfare.

Daniel names angels. Michael. Gabriel. Revelation describes cosmic warfare, beasts, dragons, and apocalyptic imagery that makes Enoch look tame.

If fantastic content disqualifies canonicity, Daniel and Revelation fail too.

Huff’s objection applies criticisms to Enoch that would disqualify Genesis, Daniel, and Revelation.

But those books are canonical.

Why Rome Deleted

Rome didn’t remove Enoch randomly.

Enoch’s cosmology is specific. It names angels. It describes hierarchies. It provides detailed maps of heaven and earth. It gives humanity direct access to cosmic architecture.

Rome’s institutional genius was controlling access to the sacred. Priests mediate. Sacraments require church. Scripture requires interpretation by trained clergy.

Enoch gives too much direct access. It’s a manual, not a mystery. You can read it and understand the cosmic structure without priestly mediation.

That’s threatening in a way Romans or Philippians isn’t.

And the content itself posed problems.

Enoch documents Watcher technology transfer. Specific angels teaching specific forbidden knowledge. It describes the Nephilim consumption pattern. Enhanced beings devouring resources, humanity, creation, each other. It explains why enhancement leads to corruption. Capability exceeding wisdom produces structural collapse. It records what happened to the first transhumans.

They became demons.

This framework makes transhumanism recognizable as ancient rebellion. It provides the precedent Silicon Valley doesn’t know exists. It explains why enhancement through technology isn’t progress but the oldest pattern repeating.

Rome couldn’t control that narrative.

So they deleted the book.

The deletion wasn’t just about content. It was about access control.

My Assessment

I don’t outsource my thinking to experts.

I engage their arguments. I acknowledge what’s fair. I refute what’s weak.

Huff raises legitimate textual and historical questions. The manuscript tradition is messier than canonical books. Quotation alone doesn’t force canonicity. Regional disagreement existed in the early church.

But he ignores Ethiopia entirely. He applies stricter standards to Enoch than to Hebrews or Revelation. He assumes Rome’s deletions are corrections without defending that assumption. He appeals to an anti-Christian Jewish council as authoritative for Christians. He never addresses why Peter uses Enochic cosmology without anyone questioning 2 Peter.

His objections are academically respectable.

They’re also post-hoc rationalizations for a decision made on institutional grounds, not textual ones.

Ethiopia received the faith before Rome decided what to delete. One church preserved. One empire edited.

The question isn’t which books belong in the Bible.

The question is who you trust to tell you.

Read Jude 14-15 and 1 Enoch 1:9 side by side. Notice Jude’s prophetic formula language. Ask yourself whether that sounds like cultural reference or divine attribution.

Read 2 Peter 2:4. Notice the Tartarus reference. Ask where Peter got that cosmology, because it wasn’t Genesis.

Ask one brother this week: “Why do we assume Rome’s deletions were corrections?”

See what conversation opens.
